The simulation peaks at 13.76 MGD at hour 11 — two hours after the heaviest rain hour — and the storm adds 2.77 million gallons of extra water across the day. The lag is the physically important feature. Rain stops being the story quickly; what the plant and the pipes actually fight is the groundwater response, which keeps bleeding into cracked joints for hours after the sky clears, because the soil around the pipes has become a charged reservoir draining through every defect. This is why operators distrust a model that ties sewer flow directly to the rain gauge: the peak arrives late, the recession is long, and a second storm landing on still-charged soil produces a bigger response than the first. It is also why infiltration rehabilitation is evaluated on storm hydrographs rather than dry-weather flows — a relined district shows its worth in a shaved, delayed peak exactly like the one this recursion produces.
Why are traffic lights organized into a repeating cycle instead of just giving each direction the green whenever cars are waiting?

Because an intersection is a shared resource that only one movement can safely use at a time, and the cycle is the schedule that divides it. A cycle is one complete pass through every phase — main street green, main street yellow and all-red, side street green, side street yellow and all-red — and its length, commonly 60 to 120 seconds in a city, is the fundamental unit of intersection capacity. Organizing by cycle does three things a purely reactive light cannot. It guarantees every movement, including pedestrians and the side street with two cars an hour, a defined turn instead of waiting for a gap in someone else's demand. It makes the intersection predictable enough to coordinate with its neighbors, so platoons released by one light arrive at the next during green — coordination is defined as offsets between cycles, which requires cycles to exist. And it bounds delay: in a cycle system your worst wait is roughly one cycle length, while a purely demand-driven light can starve a minor approach indefinitely under heavy main-street flow. Actuated signals bend the cycle — skipping phases nobody called, ending greens early — but they bend it from inside. The cycle is the constitution; detection is just the amendment process.

A signal in Alverton runs a 90-second cycle with 8 seconds of total lost time per cycle. North-south demand is 620 vehicles per hour and east-west is 410. Splitting the effective green in proportion to demand, how much green does each direction get?

After lost time, the cycle offers 82 seconds of effective green to divide. North-south carries 1030 vehicles per hour of combined demand in its share, earning 49.4 seconds, while east-west gets 32.6 seconds. Proportional splitting is the starting point of signal timing, not the finish. It equalizes the degree of saturation between approaches, which is the right fairness criterion for capacity: if one approach got less than its proportional share, it would saturate and grow a queue while the other approach's green ran partly empty. But real timing plans deviate from the raw proportions for reasons the flow numbers cannot see — a minimum green so side-street drivers believe the light works, a pedestrian interval that cannot be compressed below crossing time, a bus route whose schedule the city has promised to protect, or a downstream block too short to accept the full platoon the split would release. The proportions tell you what the traffic wants. The constraints tell you what the street allows. Timing is the negotiation between them, repeated every cycle, all day.

An approach in Kestrel Falls faces a 48-second red and arrivals of 540 vehicles per hour. How many vehicles queue by the end of the red, and how much storage length does that queue need at 24 feet per vehicle?

Arrivals of 540 vehicles per hour are 0.15 vehicles per second, so over a 48-second red the queue grows to 7.2 vehicles, needing about 173 feet of storage. That length is the design question hiding inside a simple multiplication. If the block upstream is shorter than 173 feet — or if a driveway, bus stop, or parked delivery van shortens the usable part — the tail of the queue reaches the intersection behind and starts blocking cross traffic that has a green and nowhere to go. Signal engineers therefore check the 95th-percentile queue, not the average one: arrivals are random, some cycles draw more than 7.2 vehicles, and a design that fits the average queue fails several times an hour. The queue also discharges slower than intuition suggests once green starts, because each driver in line reacts to the car ahead rather than to the light, sending a start-up wave backward through the line. The last vehicle in a long queue may begin moving ten seconds after the first one did, which is lost time the cycle has to budget for. A red light is a storage problem wearing a timing costume.
Our council wants to fix congestion by widening the main road from four lanes to six. A traffic engineer told them it might not work. How can more lanes not help?

Because congestion is usually not a lane shortage — it is a bottleneck shortage, and the bottleneck is almost always an intersection, a merge, or a bridge rather than the straight road between them. Six lanes feeding a signal that can only discharge four lanes' worth of traffic per cycle just store the same queue in a wider, more expensive parking lot. The second problem is that the queue has an address. Widen the segment before a bottleneck and you often only move the standing traffic somewhere worse — onto a short block where it spills back and gridlocks cross streets that used to flow. The third problem is behavioral: a widened road is faster at first, so trips that used other routes, other times, or transit move onto it, and latent demand fills much of the new space within a few years. None of this means widening never works — where the constraint genuinely is mid-block capacity, like a long bridge or a freight corridor, it does. It means the engineer's question comes first: where exactly does the queue form, and what discharges it? If the answer is a signal, the honest fixes are timing, turn pockets, and access management. Lanes are the most expensive way to store cars ever invented, and a city should buy them only when storage is truly what it lacks.

A lane in Port Hallis has a saturation flow of 1,850 passenger cars per hour of green and receives a green-to-cycle ratio of 0.46. Demand is 790 vehicles per hour. What is the lane's capacity, and what volume-to-capacity ratio results?

The lane's capacity is 851 vehicles per hour — saturation flow is what the lane could do with a permanent green, and the 0.46 ratio is the share of the hour it actually gets. Against demand of 790, the volume-to-capacity ratio is 0.93. That number, v/c, is the single most quoted figure in traffic engineering, and 0.93 is an uncomfortable place to live. Below about 0.85, delay is mostly the polite, cyclic kind: you wait for your turn and go. Above 0.9, the approach has almost no reserve, so ordinary randomness — a hesitant driver, a delivery van, a slightly long pedestrian phase — cannot be absorbed within the cycle and starts carrying over as a residual queue, cycle after cycle. The approach is not failing on average; it is failing on variance. This is why engineers treat v/c 1.0 as already too late rather than as the limit: a facility planned to run exactly at capacity is planned to break down daily, because demand was never going to arrive at exactly the average rate. Capacity is a mean. Traffic is a distribution.

A crosswalk in Dunmore spans 64 feet. Design walking speed is 3.5 feet per second, and the walk interval is 7 seconds before the flashing don't-walk clearance begins. How long is the clearance interval, and what is the total pedestrian phase the signal must provide?

Clearing 64 feet at 3.5 feet per second takes 18.3 seconds, so with the 7-second walk interval the signal owes pedestrians 25.3 seconds in total. That obligation is one of the hard floors in signal timing. Vehicle green can be shaved, splits can be renegotiated, but the pedestrian phase cannot go below the time a person walking at design speed needs to cross — and the design speed itself is a policy choice, since many agencies now time for 3.0 feet per second or slower near schools, hospitals, and senior housing, which stretches this same crossing's clearance past 21 seconds. On a wide arterial the pedestrian requirement can exceed what the traffic on the cross street needs, effectively setting the cycle length for everyone: vehicles on the minor street wait not for other vehicles but for the geometry of the crossing. This is the honest answer to the perennial complaint that a light 'stays red forever with nobody coming.' Sometimes somebody is coming — on foot, at 3.5 feet per second, with a legal claim on every one of those seconds. The signal is not being stupid. It is being a crossing guard.

Give me a structured comparison of the four ways the fictional city of Ternwick controls its traffic signals: fixed-time, actuated, adaptive, and transit-priority. Cover what each one senses, what it optimizes, and how it fails.

Ternwick's four signal control generations, in structure:

| Control type | What it senses | What it optimizes | Characteristic failure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fixed-time | Nothing; runs a clock-based plan by time of day | Predictability and coordination between intersections | Cannot respond to incidents, events, or a slow Tuesday; plans age as land use changes |
| Actuated | Vehicle presence on loop or video detectors, per approach | Wasted green — ends or skips phases nobody is using | A failed detector reverts an approach to maximum green or none; side streets wait for gaps in detection logic |
| Adaptive | Network-wide flows, queues, and speeds, recomputed continuously | Corridor or district throughput and delay, rebalanced in real time | Opaque decisions drivers and even staff cannot predict; garbage sensor data produces confidently wrong timing |
| Transit priority | An approaching bus or tram requesting priority | Transit schedule adherence — extends green or truncates red for the vehicle | Priority granted too often or too late in the cycle steals capacity from cross streets and can break coordination |

The progression is a trade of predictability for responsiveness. Each generation senses more and assumes less, and each inherits the previous generation's hardware as its fallback: when the adaptive layer crashes in Ternwick, the signals do not go dark — they fall back to actuated, then to fixed-time, because a dumb plan that runs beats a smart one that doesn't.

Two signals on Halloway's Grand Avenue are 1,320 feet apart, and the city wants platoons to cruise between them at 30 miles per hour. What offset, in seconds, should the downstream signal's green start after the upstream one?

Thirty miles per hour is 44 feet per second, so the platoon needs 30 seconds to travel the block — the downstream green should be offset by 30 seconds. That clean number conceals the three arguments that fill signal-timing meetings. First, which platoon: the offset serves traffic leaving the upstream light, but the platoon's tail travels slower than its head as vehicles string out, so the green window must be wide enough or timed for the middle of the pack rather than the leader. Second, which direction: an offset perfect outbound is usually wrong inbound unless block lengths and cycle length conspire kindly, so two-way progression is a compromise bought with cycle length. Third, what the platoon meets on the way: a bus dwelling at a mid-block stop, a delivery truck double-parked, or a queue left over from the last cycle all tax the ideal travel time. The offset calculation itself is trivially simple — distance over speed. The engineering is everything the calculation assumes away: that the road between the lights will behave like the empty pipe the arithmetic imagines.

A downtown block in East Sollis is 300 feet long and stores one vehicle per 25 feet. During a 55-second downstream red, traffic arrives at 900 vehicles per hour. Does the queue spill back into the upstream intersection, and by how many vehicles?

The block stores 12 vehicles. The red admits 13.75 vehicles' worth of arrivals, so the queue overruns storage by 1.75 vehicles — yes, it spills back, and the last two vehicles in line are sitting inside the upstream intersection. Spillback is the moment a traffic problem becomes a network problem. A queue on its own street is a delay; a queue standing in a box junction is a blockade, because cross traffic with a green light cannot clear, their queues grow into their own upstream boxes, and within a few cycles a district can lock into gridlock where every light is green somewhere and nothing moves anywhere. This is why the most important signal in a dense grid is often not the busiest one but the one guarding the shortest block, and why engineers sometimes deliberately meter an approach — holding cars at an upstream light where storage exists — to protect a downstream block that has none. It feels perverse to drivers, who can see open road ahead of the cars being held. The road ahead is exactly what is being protected. Storage, not speed, is the scarce resource downtown.

An approach in Marrowgate carries 1,150 vehicles per hour against a capacity of 980 for a two-hour peak. After the peak, demand falls and the approach has 130 vehicles per hour of spare capacity. How large is the residual queue when the peak ends, and how long does it take to clear?

The approach is oversaturated by 170 vehicles per hour, so across the two-hour peak it banks a residual queue of 340 vehicles — cars that arrived, were never served, and are still waiting when demand finally relaxes. Draining that backlog at 130 vehicles per hour of spare capacity takes 2.6 hours. The asymmetry is the lesson: the queue was built at 170 per hour but can only be demolished at 130 per hour, so the congestion outlives the peak that caused it by longer than the peak itself. Drivers experience this as the mystery of the 7 p.m. traffic jam on a road whose rush hour 'ends' at 6. It also corrupts measurement: an engineer counting delay during the nominal peak understates the event by the entire clearance tail. And it explains why small capacity gains at a saturated approach are worth more than large ones elsewhere — every vehicle per hour added to capacity works twice, once slowing the queue's growth during the peak and again speeding its clearance afterward. Oversaturation is a debt instrument. The peak borrows, and the evening pays.

A freeway bottleneck in Alverton can pass 4,400 vehicles per hour. Mainline demand is 3,900 and the entrance ramp wants to add 800. The ramp meter must hold total flow at capacity. What metering rate results, how often is one vehicle released, and if the ramp can store 40 vehicles, how long until its queue fills and spills onto the surface street?

The meter may release 500 vehicles per hour — one vehicle every 7.2 seconds. But the ramp wants 800, so its queue grows at 300 vehicles per hour, and 40 vehicles of storage last 8 minutes before the queue spills onto the surface street. Those three numbers are the whole politics of ramp metering. The meter does not eliminate the excess demand; it relocates the waiting from the freeway, where a breakdown would be catastrophic and system-wide, to the ramp, where it is merely miserable and local. Eight minutes of storage is the fuse on that bargain: inside it, the freeway flows and ramp drivers absorb a bounded delay; beyond it, the queue exports itself to an arterial that never agreed to the arrangement, and the surface network starts paying the freeway's bill. Metering rates are therefore set with one eye on the freeway's capacity and the other on the ramp's storage, and the honest ones admit the trade in public: somebody waits either way, and the only question the engineer actually decides is who, where, and how dangerously.

A short downtown block in Braddock Vale stores 10 queued vehicles. Each signal cycle discharges 10 vehicles from the approach, while arrivals follow a repeating pattern of 9 + (cycle mod 4) vehicles per cycle. Simulate 20 cycles of the queue and report whether and when spillback first occurs.

arguments.code:
storage = 10          # vehicles the downstream block can hold
queue = 0
for cycle in range(1, 21):
    arrivals = 9 + (cycle % 4)   # deterministic arrival pattern per cycle
    discharged = 10              # vehicles the green can serve per cycle
    queue = max(0, queue + arrivals - discharged)
    if queue > storage:
        print('spillback first occurs at cycle', cycle)
        print('queue at spillback:', queue)
        break
else:
    print('no spillback in 20 cycles')
print('arrivals pattern sums to', sum(9 + (c % 4) for c in range(1, 21)), 'vehicles over 20 cycles')

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
spillback first occurs at cycle 19
queue at spillback: 11
arrivals pattern sums to 210 vehicles over 20 cycles

The simulation shows spillback first occurring at cycle 19, when the queue reaches 11 vehicles against storage of 10. The approach is only barely oversaturated — arrivals average 10.5 vehicles per cycle against a discharge of 10 — so a coarse hourly analysis calls this a slow leak, not an emergency: half a vehicle per cycle of excess. But watch the mechanism. The queue does not grow smoothly; it ratchets. The cycles drawing 12 arrivals add two vehicles each, the 9-arrival cycles repay only one, and the debt therefore climbs in steps, two up and one down, until the block's storage is exhausted late in the run. This is why cycle-by-cycle simulation earns its place next to average-based analysis: storage failures are caused by sequences, not averages. A block does not care that the imbalance was small. It cares that at one specific moment, eleven vehicles wanted to stand where ten fit — and the eleventh was standing in somebody else's intersection, converting a half-vehicle-per-cycle rounding error into gridlock.
Transit schedules talk about 'headway' instead of just saying how many buses per hour. What is a headway, and why do transit people prefer it?

A headway is the time between consecutive vehicles on a route — if buses come every 12 minutes, the headway is 12 minutes. Its reciprocal is frequency: a 12-minute headway is 5 buses per hour. Riders and planners prefer headway because it is the number the passenger actually experiences. Nobody at a stop thinks in buses per hour; they think 'the next one comes in about twelve minutes,' and their average wait, when they arrive at random, is half the headway. Headway also exposes the quality that matters most: regularity. Two services can both run 6 buses per hour, but one spaces them evenly at 10-minute headways while the other sends two together and then nothing for 20 minutes. The frequency is identical and the service is not — the second has an effective headway, for waiting purposes, far worse than 10 minutes, which is why agencies measure headway adherence rather than counting departures. Frequency is an accounting number, useful for budgets and fleet math. Headway is a promise made to a person standing at a pole, and transit people prefer it because it is written in the unit the promise is kept or broken in.

Hallis Transit's Route 9 takes 84 minutes for a complete round trip including layover, and the agency wants a bus every 12 minutes. How many buses does the schedule require, and how many should the agency own if it keeps a 20 percent spare ratio?

The schedule requires 7 buses in service at once: with a round trip of 84 minutes and a departure every 12 minutes, seven buses must be somewhere on the loop at all times or a gap opens. Owning only seven would be a plan that works exclusively on days when nothing breaks, so with a 20 percent spare ratio the fleet requirement becomes 8.4 — in practice nine buses, because buses are bought whole. The spare ratio is not padding; it is the maintenance program expressed as a number. Buses cycle through inspections, repairs, cleaning, and the occasional fender-bender, and a fleet with no spares converts every shop visit into a missed trip. Notice the lever hiding in the arithmetic: the requirement is set by cycle time divided by headway, so anything that lengthens the round trip — congestion, slower boarding, a detour — silently demands more buses to hold the same timetable. A route that slows by 12 minutes has, in effect, spent a bus. Traffic engineers and transit planners are often arguing about the same vehicle from opposite ends of that equation.
Route 4 in Varenne runs buses every 7.5 minutes, and each bus has a crush capacity of 62 passengers. What is the route's maximum passenger capacity per hour in one direction?

At a 7.5-minute headway the route dispatches 8 buses per hour, and at 62 passengers each that is 496 passengers per hour per direction — the route's line capacity. The number deserves suspicion in both directions. It overstates what riders will tolerate, because crush capacity means standees packed at densities where dwell times balloon and the schedule dissolves; planners usually design to a load factor well below it, treating the last third of the bus as emergency reserve rather than product. And it understates what the corridor could carry, because capacity is not a property of the bus but of the system: the same vehicles at a 5-minute headway, or in a lane where signals and cars cannot interfere, carry proportionally more. This is why capacity arguments in transit are really headway arguments in disguise. The vehicle is bought once; the headway is bought every day, with drivers' wages, forever. When a city asks how much capacity it can afford, it is asking how small a headway it can fund — the arithmetic of buses per hour is just the visible tip of a labor budget.
Why do buses on the same route bunch up in pairs — one packed, one empty right behind it — instead of staying evenly spaced?

Because an evenly spaced bus route is an unstable equilibrium, and the bunching is the system falling off it. Imagine two buses on a 10-minute headway. The leader is delayed slightly — a wheelchair securement, a fare dispute, one bad light — and now the gap ahead of it has been growing for 12 minutes instead of 10, so more passengers have accumulated at each stop. More passengers means longer boarding, which delays it further, which grows the gap further: a positive feedback loop with the timetable as its victim. The follower has the mirror-image experience. It is now only 8 minutes behind the leader instead of 10, so it finds stops nearly empty — the leader just collected everyone — and it runs faster and faster until it is on the leader's bumper, carrying almost nobody. The pair then travels as a unit: one bus doing all the work at crush load, one doing none, and passengers at stops experience a 20-minute gap followed by two buses at once. Dispatchers fight it with holding — deliberately delaying the follower at terminals or timing points — which feels perverse to the riders being held but is the only move that breaks the loop, because the instability lives in the spacing, and only spacing discipline cures it.

Two buses on a Varenne route are scheduled 8 minutes apart, giving riders an average wait of half the headway. After bunching, the gaps alternate between 1 minute and 15 minutes. Using the formula average wait = sum of squared gaps / (2 × sum of gaps), what does the average wait become?

With even 8-minute spacing the average wait would be 4 minutes. After bunching, the same two buses per 16 minutes produce an average wait of 7.06 minutes — the formula's unrounded value is 7.0625 — nearly double, with zero change in the number of buses, drivers, or fuel. The squaring in the formula is the whole story. Passengers do not arrive in proportion to the number of gaps; they arrive in proportion to the length of gaps, and a passenger's wait is proportional to the gap they landed in, so long gaps are double-counted — more people land in them and each waits longer. A 15-minute gap contributes 225 to the numerator; the 1-minute gap contributes 1. This is why a transit agency can honestly report running 100 percent of scheduled trips while riders honestly report the service collapsing. Both are describing the same buses. The agency is counting vehicles; the passengers are experiencing gaps. Reliability metrics exist to close exactly this gap between the operator's arithmetic and the rider's, and headway regularity — not trip count — is the metric that does it.

A Hallis Transit bus needs 96 minutes of running time for a round trip but is scheduled on a 110-minute cycle. How much recovery time is built in, what percentage of running time is it, and what happens on a trip that arrives 11 minutes late?

The schedule carries 14 minutes of recovery — 14.6 percent on top of running time. Recovery is the schedule's savings account: it exists to absorb the ordinary insults of a trip — a slow boarding, a freight train, a passenger who needs the lift — so the bus can still depart its next trip on time. A bus arriving 11 minutes late spends almost the whole account, leaving 3 minutes to turn around, which means the next trip starts essentially naked: any further delay passes straight through to passengers as a late departure, and if the pattern repeats across trips the deficit compounds into the bunching and gaps the riders remember. Agencies argue endlessly over the right percentage because recovery looks, to a budget reviewer, like paying drivers to sit. Too little and the timetable is fiction by 9 a.m.; too much and the agency is buying buses and hours to provide standing time. The honest framing is that recovery is not slack in the schedule — it is the schedule's insurance premium, priced in minutes, against a city that never has the same day twice.

Give me a structured comparison of city bus, bus rapid transit, light rail, and metro using a fictional agency's planning figures: vehicles per hour, capacity per vehicle, resulting passengers per hour per direction, and what right-of-way each needs.

Planning comparison from the fictional Hallis Transit figures (for structure, not quotation):

| Mode | Vehicles per hour | Capacity per vehicle | Passengers per hour per direction | Right-of-way |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| City bus | 30 | 60 | 1,800 | Mixed traffic |
| Bus rapid transit | 40 | 90 | 3,600 | Dedicated lanes, off-board fare payment |
| Light rail | 20 trains (2 cars) | 150 per car | 6,000 | Mostly exclusive, some shared street running |
| Metro | 30 trains (6 cars) | 140 per car | 25,200 | Fully grade-separated |

How to read it: capacity grows by attacking different terms of the same multiplication. The city bus is frequency-limited — stops and signals will not let it run much above 30 per hour in mixed traffic. BRT buys bigger vehicles and a protected path so frequency and size rise together. Light rail couples cars into trains, trading frequency for consist size. The metro removes every surface conflict, letting frequency and train length compound at once. The right-of-way column is the real price list: each step's capacity is purchased by taking space from other users or building above and below them, which is why mode debates in city councils are land-use debates wearing a transit costume.

East Sollis Transit spent $4.85 million operating its bus network last year and collected $1.32 million in fares, at an average fare of $1.05. What was its farebox recovery ratio, how many boardings does the fare revenue imply, and what subsidy did each boarding require?

Fares covered 27.2 percent of operating cost — the farebox recovery ratio. At an average fare of $1.05, the revenue implies 1257143 boardings, and dividing the uncovered cost across them gives a subsidy of $2.81 per boarding. That per-boarding figure is the one worth arguing about, because it converts an ideological debate into an engineering comparison. Every alternative way of moving that passenger has a price too: the road space, parking, and congestion a transit rider does not consume are costs the city does not pay, and a subsidy per boarding can be compared directly against the cost per trip of the road capacity the city would otherwise build. The recovery ratio itself mostly measures local policy, not competence — it falls when a city chooses low fares, free transfers, or deep discount passes, and rises when it chooses to price riders away. Two agencies with identical operations can post wildly different ratios because their councils made different choices about who pays. The ratio is a mirror held up to the fare policy. The subsidy per boarding is the bill for the mobility itself.

A Dunmore bus route makes 14 stops per trip with an average dwell of 22 seconds, on a run scheduled at 62 minutes. How much of the trip is spent dwelling, in seconds, minutes, and percent, and how much time would cutting average dwell to 15 seconds save?

The bus spends 308 seconds — 5.1 minutes, or 8.3 percent of its 62-minute schedule — standing still with its doors open. Cutting average dwell to 15 seconds would save 98 seconds per trip. Dwell is the most underestimated quantity in bus operations because it is nobody's department: it belongs partly to the vehicle (door width, step height), partly to the fare system (paying on board is the slowest known method of collecting money), partly to stop design (a bus that must merge back into traffic loses more time re-entering than it spent boarding), and partly to the passengers themselves, whose numbers the agency is trying to grow. Yet it compounds like interest. Ninety-eight seconds a trip is a minute and a half of cycle time, and cycle time divided by headway is fleet size — shave enough dwell across a network and you have, in effect, found buses you did not have to buy. This is why off-board fare payment and all-door boarding, which sound like passenger-experience frills, are actually capacity investments with a payback measured in vehicles.

A 6-mile bus route in Ternwick currently stops every 0.25 miles. The agency proposes spacing stops every 0.4 miles instead. Each stop costs the bus 28 seconds in deceleration, dwell, and re-entry. How many stops does each pattern have, and how much running time does the change save per trip?

The current pattern has 24 stops; the proposed one has 15. Removing nine stops saves 252 seconds — 4.2 minutes — per trip. That is the visible half of the trade. The invisible half is walking: spacing stops 0.4 miles apart raises the average walk to a stop from roughly an eighth of a mile to a fifth, and for riders with groceries, children, or bad knees, the route effectively moves farther away even as it gets faster. The riders who remain gain twice — their bus is quicker and its schedule is more reliable, because fewer stops means fewer chances for delay to compound. The riders who quietly disappear from the counts do not appear in the agency's time-savings table at all. Mature stop-spacing programs handle this by protecting stops near hospitals, senior housing, and transfer points regardless of spacing math, and by counting the change honestly: some of the celebrated ridership 'growth' after consolidation is the same riders walking further, and some of the loss is people for whom the walk became the trip. The 28 seconds is real. So is the fifth of a mile. A good agency publishes both numbers.

Hallis Transit's buses log 310 revenue hours in a day, plus 38 hours of deadhead (driving empty to and from the garage and between routes) and 24 hours of layover. What are total platform hours, what share is deadhead, and what does a platform day cost at $118 per platform hour?

Total platform time is 372 hours, of which deadhead is 10.2 percent, and the day costs $43896 at the platform-hour rate. Platform hours are the honest denominator of transit finance because drivers are paid for all of them — the clock starts when the bus leaves the garage, not when the first passenger boards. Deadhead is the purest form of the cost: fuel, wages, and wear spent moving an empty vehicle that exists only because the garage, the route start, and the route end are in three different places. Agencies attack it geographically — siting garages near route terminals, interlining routes so a bus finishing one run begins another nearby instead of returning empty — and the gains are real but bounded by the city's shape. The reason the figure belongs in public is the comparison it enables: two agencies can run identical revenue hours at wildly different cost because one inherited a well-placed garage and the other inherited a cheap parcel at the edge of town. The empty miles are a land-use decision from decades ago, still being paid for by the hour.

Model two buses that start evenly spaced, 10 minutes apart, on a route where each bus's dwell grows with the number of waiting passengers, and the leader steadily loses a little time each stop to the follower. Run the 30-stop simulation and report the final spacing.

arguments.code:
gap_ahead = 10.0   # minutes of passengers accumulated for the leader
gap_behind = 10.0  # minutes accumulated for the follower
for stop in range(30):
    dwell_a = 0.4 + 0.06*gap_ahead    # leader dwells longer the more people wait
    dwell_b = 0.4 + 0.06*gap_behind
    gap_ahead = gap_ahead + (dwell_b - dwell_a)*0.5 + 0.35   # leader keeps losing time
    gap_behind = 20.0 - gap_ahead
print('final gap ahead of leader (min):', round(gap_ahead, 1))
print('final gap ahead of follower (min):', round(gap_behind, 1))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
final gap ahead of leader (min): 14.9
final gap ahead of follower (min): 5.1

After 30 stops the leader's gap has stretched to 14.9 minutes while the follower's has collapsed to 5.1 minutes — the pair has collapsed most of the way toward bunching, the follower now running in the leader's slipstream instead of on its own schedule. The simulation's engine is a single asymmetry: dwell time depends on the gap ahead, so any disturbance is self-amplifying in both directions at once. The leader, serving a longer accumulation of passengers, dwells longer and falls further behind; the follower, serving the leader's leftovers, dwells less and catches up. Nothing in the model is malicious or broken — no breakdown, no traffic, no bad driver — and the timetable still dissolves, which is the deepest fact about bus reliability: even spacing is not a state a route rests in but a state it must be actively held in. That is why control strategies intervene on the spacing itself — holding the follower at timing points, short-turning a bus to fill a gap, or instructing a driver to skip stops when running as the second half of a pair. You cannot schedule your way out of an unstable equilibrium. You can only govern it, continuously, all day.
Why do garbage truck routes seem so oddly specific — same streets, same order, every week? Why not just send trucks wherever the trash is?

Because the trash is everywhere, in roughly the same amount, every week — residential waste is one of the most predictable flows a city manages. A household sets out a similar cart on a similar schedule indefinitely, so the problem is not finding the trash but visiting ten thousand known points with the fewest miles, turns, and hours. The route is a solved puzzle: stops sequenced so the truck makes mostly right turns, never crosses its own path, fills its body just as it reaches the last streets before the disposal run, and balances hours against the other routes so all crews finish together. The specificity you notice is the solution's fingerprint. Routes also encode hard constraints invisible from the curb: streets a loaded truck cannot climb when icy, alleys too narrow for the arm, school zones avoided at bell times, and the one-way grid downtown. When a city rebalances routes — usually after growth or a new truck type — residents experience it as their pickup day changing, which is why it is politically delicate despite being pure logistics. The odd specificity is not bureaucracy. It is an optimization that has been running so long it looks like a custom, and the custom is load-bearing: improvise the order and the truck comes home at dark, half full, having crossed the city twice.

A residential route in Ossbury serves 1,150 stops averaging 34 pounds of setout each. The packer truck's legal payload is 13 tons. How many tons does the full route generate, and at what share of the route will the truck be full?

The route generates 39100 pounds — 19.55 tons — against a legal payload of 13 tons, so the truck fills up at about 66.5 percent of its stops and must break off, haul to disposal, and return for the remainder. That mid-route unload is one of the most expensive events in collection, because the truck spends it doing everything except collecting: driving loaded to the disposal site, queuing, tipping, and driving back empty to resume a route that is now an hour older. Route designers treat payload as a geography problem. Assign the truck a slightly smaller route and it finishes in one load but underuses its capacity every day; assign a bigger one and the second trip eats the savings. The sweet spot shifts with the seasons — setouts swell after holidays and during yard-waste peaks — which is why good operations keep a couple of swing routes whose stops can migrate between trucks. The number on the door, 13 tons, looks like a vehicle specification. On the route sheet it is a deadline: everything after 66.5 percent is a second trip, and second trips are where collection budgets go to die.

Braddock Vale collected 96,400 tons of residential material last year: 21,300 tons recycled, 9,800 tons composted, and the rest landfilled. What is the city's diversion rate, and how many tons went to landfill?

Braddock Vale diverted 31100 tons and landfilled 65300 tons, for a diversion rate of 32.3 percent. The rate is the industry's headline metric and also its most gamed one, because every term in it is a definition. Does 'collected' include construction debris a contractor hauled privately? Does composted yard waste count at the scale house or after the moisture cooks off? Is a ton of glass shipped to a recycler 'recycled' when it leaves the curb, when it reaches the materials recovery facility, or when a manufacturer actually melts it — three different tons, honestly measured, shrinking at each step. Cities chasing a target learn to move the boundary rather than the material. The number's legitimate use is internal and longitudinal: the same city, the same definitions, year over year, where a rising rate really does mean trucks are routing differently. Compared across cities it measures accounting conventions. The tons, at least, are tons — 65300 of them went into a hole, and the hole is the one constituency in waste management that never argues about definitions.
Why would a city unload garbage from collection trucks into other trucks at a transfer station? Hauling the same trash twice sounds wasteful.

It sounds wasteful because the two hauls look identical, but they are different products. The collection truck is a specialized, expensive machine — a compactor body, a robotic arm, a crew — that is only earning its keep while it is at the curb lifting carts. Every mile it spends driving to a distant landfill is a mile its arm is not lifting, and its payload, maybe 13 tons, is small. The transfer trailer is the opposite: a dumb, cheap box holding 25 tons or more, pulled by an ordinary tractor, doing nothing but highway miles. The transfer station is where the expensive machine hands its load to the cheap one, the way a local delivery van hands parcels to a long-haul truck. The economics turn on distance. If the landfill is across town, direct haul wins and transfer stations make no sense. As disposal sites retreat — and they always retreat, because nobody permits a new landfill near a city — the collection fleet spends more of its day driving, and at some distance the handoff pays for the building, the tipping floor, and the second handling. The twice-haul is really a specialization: stop spending a quarter-million-dollar machine's hours on highway miles that a plain trailer does better, and let each vehicle do the leg it was built for.

A restaurant in Marrowgate generates 420 pounds of waste per day, and its dumpster holds 1,500 pounds before it is effectively full. How many days does the dumpster take to fill, and how many pickups per week does the restaurant need at minimum?

The dumpster fills in 3.57 days. Across a week the restaurant generates 2940 pounds, which is 1.96 dumpster-loads — so two pickups a week is the arithmetic minimum, and the schedule matters as much as the count. Two pickups spaced evenly, say Monday and Thursday, leave maximum gaps of four days against a 3.57 day fill time: cutting it close enough that one banquet weekend overflows the enclosure, and an overflowing dumpster is not a private problem — it is windblown litter, a health-code conversation, and a landlord dispute in a shared alley. This is why commercial collection is sold as a joint decision about container size and frequency: a bigger dumpster and a smaller one picked up twice as often can carry the same weekly volume at different prices, and the right answer depends on the site's space and the hauler's route density in that neighborhood. The fill-time calculation is the customer's half of the negotiation. The hauler's half is knowing that a stop already on Tuesday's route costs far less to add than a special trip — the dumpster is priced by its position on someone else's route as much as by its size.

Give me a structured comparison of the three residential and commercial collection systems a city like the fictional Varenne might run: manual rear-load, automated side-load, and front-load. Cover crew size, stops per hour, the container each uses, and the main drawback of each. Use fictional planning figures.

Varenne's three collection systems, using the city's planning figures:

| System | Crew | Stops per hour | Container | Main drawback |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Manual rear-load | 3 | 55 | Bags and loose cans at the curb | Highest injury rate — lifting, riding the step, traffic exposure |
| Automated side-load | 1 | 110 | Standardized wheeled cart, set out with clearance | Useless where cars park against the curb or in alleys; cart fleet is a capital program of its own |
| Front-load | 1 | 28 (commercial stops) | Steel dumpsters, 2–8 cubic yards | Forks need overhead clearance and a straight approach; noisy at 5 a.m. behind apartments |

The pattern is labor traded for standardization. The manual system accepts any container a resident owns, which is precisely its cost: human backs absorb the variety. Automation doubles route speed and cuts injuries dramatically, but only by conscripting every household into the same cart, placed the same way, on streets the arm can reach — a political program disguised as a truck purchase. Front-load is the commercial cousin: few stops, heavy lifts, and a schedule written around business hours and alley geometry. Cities rarely choose one system; they inherit all three, sorted by the era and density of each neighborhood.

The regional landfill serving Kestrel Falls has 4.2 million cubic yards of permitted airspace left. It receives waste that compacts to 310,000 cubic yards per year, and daily cover soil consumes an additional 15 percent of airspace. How many years of life remain?

True airspace consumption is 356500 cubic yards per year once cover soil is counted, so the site has 11.8 years of life. The cover-soil term is the one public debates always miss. A landfill is not a hole you fill with trash alone; each day's waste must be buried under soil to control litter, odor, and vectors, and that soil occupies the same permitted volume as the waste it covers. Roughly one year in eight of this site's remaining life will be spent storing dirt. The 11.8 year figure is therefore also a countdown for decisions with very long lead times: siting and permitting a replacement landfill or a transfer-and-rail operation is a decade-long project in most jurisdictions, which means the conversation has to start essentially now, while the site still looks half empty. Landfill life also creates a strange pricing politics — as the end approaches, the remaining airspace becomes more valuable, tipping fees rise, and diversion programs that looked uneconomic suddenly clear their hurdle. The hole is an asset that depletes. Cities that track its life honestly, cover soil included, are the ones not holding emergency meetings in year eleven.

A materials recovery facility serving Alverton takes in 820 tons of curbside recycling per day, but 18.5 percent comes out as residue — contamination and unmarketable material — that must be landfilled at $58 per ton. How much residue is that per day, and what does its disposal cost daily?

The facility landfills 151.7 tons of residue a day, at a disposal cost of about $8799 daily — before counting the double handling of trucking it there. Residue is where the recycling system's optimism meets its physics. Residents, wanting to do right, toss in garden hoses, plastic bags, greasy pizza boxes, and batteries — 'wishcycling' — and the facility must pay people and machines to remove them, because a single contaminated bale can be rejected by the buyer who was supposed to pay for it. The residue rate therefore prices education as surely as it prices sorting equipment: every point of contamination is worth roughly eight tons a day here, plus the disposal fee, plus the lost commodity revenue on material ruined by contact with contaminants. It also explains the otherwise puzzling strictness of recycling rules. A program that accepts everything accepts, in practice, a residue stream it must landfill at retail prices. The honest public message is not 'when in doubt, throw it in.' It is the opposite — when in doubt, keep it out — because the facility's residue line is where good intentions are weighed and billed.

Dunmore's five Tuesday collection routes take 9.2, 7.4, 8.8, 6.9, and 8.1 hours. What is the total and the mean route time, what is the spread between the longest and shortest routes, and why does the spread matter more than the mean for the overtime budget?

The five routes total 40.4 hours for a mean of 8.08 hours, but the spread between longest and shortest is 2.3 hours — and the spread, not the mean, writes the overtime check. Crews are paid against the shift, not the average: the 9.2-hour route earns 1.2 hours of overtime every Tuesday while the 6.9-hour crew finishes early, and the city cannot average one crew's evening against another's. Worse, the long route is where service failures breed — a truck that is behind at hour eight skips the alley it cannot afford, and its residents call. Route balancing is therefore an exercise in equalizing the maximum, which usually means moving stops from the long route to the short one until geography pushes back: stops are not fluid, a street belongs to whichever truck passes it, and the boundary streets are few. The mean of 8.08 hours looks healthy in a budget presentation. The 2.3 hour spread is what the operation actually feels like, and any manager quoting the mean without the spread is telling you the routes are balanced in a sense no crew would recognize.

A collection truck in East Sollis currently hauls directly to a landfill 38 miles away, averaging 31 mph on the round trip plus 0.4 hours tipping and queuing. A proposed transfer station is 6 miles away (28 mph average, 0.25 hours to tip). Compare the non-collection time per load under each option and the daily saving across 14 loads.

Direct haul burns 2.85 hours per load on driving and tipping; the transfer run burns 0.68 hours. The difference is 2.17 hours per load, and across 14 loads a day the fleet recovers 30.4 truck-hours daily — the equivalent of roughly four extra collection trucks that the city does not have to buy, crew, or maintain. Those recovered hours are the entire case for the transfer station, and they also expose its limit: the saving is bought with a building, a tipping floor, transfer trailers, and a second handling of every ton, so the calculation only clears its costs when the haul is long and the tonnage is large. Note what the comparison leaves out — the line-haul from transfer station to landfill still happens, just in 25-ton trailers at highway speed with one driver instead of five collection crews. The system's total driving may not even fall. What falls is expensive driving: hours in specialized trucks with lifting arms idle on the highway. Transfer economics is the art of making sure the costly machine never does the cheap machine's job.
When it snows, the main roads get plowed again and again while my side street waits a day. Why does the city prioritize like that instead of treating every street equally?

Because in a storm the city's plows are a scarce resource moving slower than the problem, and equal treatment would mean equal failure everywhere. Priority tiers exist to protect the trips the whole city depends on first: arterials carry the ambulances, fire trucks, buses, and the sheer majority of traffic, and they include the hills and bridges where a stalled car blocks everyone. If plows spread themselves evenly, every street would be half-plowed all the time and the emergency network would be as stuck as the cul-de-sacs. So the tiers sequence the work — arterials and bus routes continuously during the storm, collectors next, residential streets once the snow stops or reaches a depth trigger — and the side street's day of waiting is the visible price of the ambulance's clear run. The tiers are also a promise the city can be held to: published maps tell you which class your street is in and what service level to expect, which converts an argument about favoritism into a checkable fact. The system is not claiming your street does not matter. It is claiming that in a resource crunch, order matters, and the order was decided in advance, in public, instead of by which neighborhood calls loudest during the storm.

A snow route in Kestrel Falls covers 46 lane-miles, and the plow averages an effective 11 miles per hour accounting for turns, intersections, and refills. How long does one pass take, and how many full passes fit in a 9-hour storm?

One pass takes 4.18 hours, so a 9-hour storm allows 2.2 passes — two full passes and a partial third. That arithmetic quietly governs snow strategy. If snow falls at an inch an hour, the route accumulates over four inches between the plow's visits, which is why operators talk about cycle time the way transit people talk about headways: it is the interval at which service repeats, and everything residents experience follows from it. Shortening the cycle means more trucks on shorter routes, which is a budget decision made in summer and felt in January. The effective speed of 11 mph is also worth respecting — a plow's dashboard speed on a straight stretch might be 25, but the route average is devoured by turns, backing into cul-de-sacs, intersections taken slowly with the blade down, and the trip back to the salt dome. Residents who time the truck past their house and extrapolate are always disappointed. The route is not a lap; it is a obstacle course run with a wall of snow building on the right side, and 4.18 hours is what the course actually costs.
Ossbury spreads salt at 280 pounds per lane-mile over 310 lane-miles in a typical event. How much salt is that per event in pounds and tons, and how many such events does a 1,900-ton stockpile cover?

A typical event consumes 86800 pounds — 43.4 tons — and the 1,900-ton stockpile therefore covers 43.8 events. That events-per-stockpile figure is the number winter managers actually live by, because salt is bought in summer, delivered by barge and rail on schedules set months ahead, and cannot be conjured in February when every city in the region is drawing down at once. A winter is not budgeted in tons; it is budgeted in storms, and the stockpile converts weather uncertainty into inventory risk: too few events and the city stored salt it did not need (cheap insurance, easily defended), too many and it is rationing in March — spreading at reduced rates, prioritizing hills and intersections — precisely when freeze-thaw cycles make roads treacherous. The application rate itself is a compromise struck with the watershed: 280 pounds per lane-mile is enough to keep the salt brine working at typical storm temperatures, but every pound eventually washes into streams and groundwater, so the modern trend is to spend on pre-wetting and brine to make fewer pounds behave like more. The stockpile number looks like logistics. It is actually the city's winter risk tolerance, expressed in tons.

Before a forecast storm, Ternwick applies salt brine at 32 gallons per lane-mile over 240 lane-miles. The brine carries about 2.3 pounds of salt per gallon. How many gallons are applied, and how much salt does that represent in pounds and tons?

The pre-treatment lays down 7680 gallons of brine carrying about 17664 pounds of salt — 8.83 tons. Compare that with the dry-salt response to the same storm after it starts, which on Ternwick's network would run several times that tonnage, and the point of anti-icing appears: a thin brine film applied before the snow bonds to the pavement prevents the bond rather than breaking it, and prevention is chemically far cheaper than cure. The salt is also placed with an accuracy dry spreading cannot match — a liquid goes where the nozzle points, while rock salt bounces and scatters off the crown of the road, with studies routinely finding a third of it in the gutter before a tire ever touches it. The catch is forecast dependence. Brine applied before a storm that veers away is wasted, and rain that arrives before the snow washes the film off entirely, so anti-icing is a bet placed on the forecast with the stockpile as the stake. De-icing after the fact is the conservative strategy: expensive, certain, and always late. Brine programs are what it looks like when a snow operation decides to trade certainty for efficiency — and buys better forecasting with part of the winnings.

Give me a structured summary of the three snow response levels used by the fictional city of Halloway: what triggers each, how much of the fleet deploys, and what service target the city promises at each level.

Halloway's snow plan, by response level:

| Level | Trigger | Fleet deployed | Service target |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 — Nuisance | Under 2 inches, no ice warning | 40% of plows, brine trucks pre-treating | Arterials bare within 4 hours of storm end; residential streets untreated unless icy |
| 2 — Working storm | 2–6 inches or any freezing rain | 75% of plows, full salt stock rotation | Arterials bare within 3 hours; collectors passable during the storm; residential plowed within 24 hours of storm end |
| 3 — Emergency | Over 6 inches, blizzard conditions, or ice storm | 100% of fleet plus contractors, 12-hour shifts | Life-safety network (hospital and fire routes) kept open continuously; all streets passable within 48 hours; parking ban enforced for curb-to-curb clearing |

The levels are really a pre-negotiated treaty between the weather and the budget. Each level commits money — overtime, contractor callouts, salt — that cannot be unspent if the storm underperforms, so the triggers are written to be callable by a duty officer at 3 a.m. without a meeting. Notice that the promises degrade gracefully rather than uniformly: Level 3 does not promise everyone less of the same service, it explicitly narrows the guarantee to the life-safety network and tells everyone else to wait two days. A snow plan that promises everything at every level is not a plan; it is a hope with a logo on it.

Alverton owns 64 plow trucks, but 9 are in the shop on the morning of a forecast storm. The snow plan needs 58 trucks to cover all routes simultaneously. What is the fleet's availability percentage, and is the plan covered?

Only 55 trucks are available — an availability of 85.9 percent — and the plan needs 58, so Alverton starts the storm 3 trucks short. That shortfall is the number that decides how the storm feels. Three uncovered routes do not mean three streets wait; they mean three routes get folded into neighboring ones, lengthening those cycles, so a whole district's service degrades by the merged routes' extra hours. The availability percentage deserves attention because it is the meeting point of two budgets that rarely meet: the fleet was bought by a capital process that counts trucks, but it is made available by a maintenance process that counts mechanics, parts, and shop bays. A city can own a magnificent fleet and field a mediocre one. Readiness also decays exactly when it matters — trucks break during storms, under load, in the cold — so a plan that starts at exactly 58 of 58 has no storm in it at all. Alverton's managers have three honest options, in order of preference: pull the contractor clause before the first flake, pre-position the shortfall on the lowest-priority routes and say so publicly, or run longer shifts and accept slower cycles. The dishonest option is to publish the plan as if 58 were available. The storm will correct the record by morning.

After an exceptional storm, Varenne hauls 1,850 truckloads of snow from its downtown, each load 14 cubic yards, to a melt pit that processes 220 cubic yards per hour. How much snow is hauled, and how long must the melter run?

The haul totals 25900 cubic yards of snow, and the melter needs 117.7 hours — nearly five days of continuous running — to dispose of it. Those numbers explain why snow hauling is the last resort of urban snow management, deployed only where snow has literally nowhere else to be: dense downtowns where windrows would block storefronts and intersections for weeks. Everything about it is expensive. Snow is mostly air, so trucks haul a product that is 90 percent void; it must be loaded by machine, driven across town, and then melted with fuel or stored on land valuable enough to be missed. The melt rate is the binding constraint — the city can always find more trucks, but the pit processes what it processes, and 117.7 hours of melt time means the operation spans multiple subsequent weather cycles. Cities that haul regularly therefore treat snow storage as land banking: peripheral lots, held all year for a few weeks of use, whose emptiness in July looks like waste and whose existence in February is the difference between a downtown that reopens and one that waits for spring. The melter's slow arithmetic is why that land is worth holding.

Accounting for one storm in Dunmore: labor 3,900 hours at $46 per hour, salt 212 tons at $78 per ton, fuel 9,800 gallons at $3.85 per gallon. What did the storm cost in total, and per lane-mile across the city's 640 lane-miles?

Labor came to $179400, salt to $16536, and fuel to $37730 — a storm total of $233666, or about $365 per lane-mile. The composition matters more than the total. Labor is over three-quarters of the cost, which means a snow budget is mostly a staffing instrument: the decision that drives the bill is not how much salt to buy but how many people to keep on shift, for how long, at overtime rates, against a forecast that may not verify. This is why storm accounting is always slightly unfair — a city that staffs up for a storm that misses pays nearly the full labor bill for bare pavement, and gets mocked for waste by the same public that would flay it for being caught short. Per-lane-mile costing at least makes storms comparable across years and cities of different sizes, separating the price of the weather from the size of the network. But it should be read with the service level attached: $365 per lane-mile bought Dunmore a specific promise about when streets would be bare. A cheaper storm bill is always available — it is called a lower promise, and residents get to choose it only in the summer, in the budget, never during the storm itself.
What is a 'feeder' in a city's power distribution system? The word sounds like it belongs in a factory.

A feeder is one of the main circuits that carries power out of a substation into a neighborhood — think of the substation as a heart and the feeders as its major arteries. The substation takes high-voltage transmission power and steps it down; each feeder then distributes that power along a corridor of streets, with smaller lateral lines branching off to individual blocks and service drops to buildings. A feeder typically serves a few thousand customers and carries a few megawatts. The concept matters because almost everything about distribution operations is organized by feeder. Outages are reported by which feeder tripped. Reliability statistics are kept per feeder, so the utility knows which corridors are its problem children. Load forecasts, switching plans, and maintenance budgets are all feeder-shaped. When a tree takes down a line and 2,000 homes go dark, what usually happened is a protective device on their feeder opened the circuit to isolate the fault — the feeder sacrificed itself to keep the damage local. And when crews 'tie feeders together' during a restoration, they are using the switches between adjacent feeders to backfeed a healthy section from a neighboring artery. Learn the feeder map of a city and you have learned the skeleton its electric life hangs on; every other term in distribution is plumbing attached to those arteries.
A feeder in Port Hallis peaks at 8.6 megawatts but averages 5.16 megawatts over the day. What is its load factor, and how much energy does it deliver in 24 hours?

The load factor is 60 percent — average load divided by peak — and the feeder delivers 123.84 megawatt-hours across the day. Load factor is the utilization rate of the electricity system, and it is the quiet driver of power prices. Every wire, transformer, and switch on that feeder must be sized for the 8.6-megawatt peak, because equipment does not care about averages; it cares about the worst fifteen minutes of the year. But the system only sells the average. A feeder at 60 percent load factor is, in effect, a factory that runs its machines three-fifths of the time while paying for all of them — the capital cost of the peak is spread over the energy of the average. This is why utilities care so much about the shape of demand, not just its size: air conditioning that all switches on at 4 p.m. creates a needle peak that is ruinously expensive to serve, while the same energy consumed overnight would ride nearly free on idle capacity. Demand charges, time-of-use rates, and load-control programs are all attempts to buy load factor — to pay customers to move their megawatt-hours from the peak the system must build for to the valley it has already built.

A utility in Marrowgate serves 28,000 customers. Last quarter it recorded three sustained outages: 1,240 customers out for 95 minutes, 860 for 150 minutes, and 2,300 for 42 minutes. Compute the quarter's SAIDI contribution in minutes per customer and the SAIFI contribution in interruptions per customer.

The three events accumulate 343400 customer-minutes of interruption. Spread across all 28,000 customers, that is a SAIDI contribution of 12.26 minutes per customer, and since 4,400 customers were interrupted at all, a SAIFI contribution of 0.157 interruptions per customer. The two indices are a matched pair because each hides what the other reveals. SAIDI weights by duration, so it is dominated by the long 150-minute event even though it touched the fewest people. SAIFI counts heads and ignores minutes, so it treats a 42-minute outage and a 10-hour one as identical sins. A utility can game either alone — restoring many small outages quickly flatters SAIFI while a few neighborhoods rot, and vice versa — which is why regulators demand both, and why the honest conversation adds a third question neither answers: who. Averages launder distribution. If the same 1,240 customers appear in every quarter's outage list, the system's 12.26 minutes is a fiction for them; they live in a different, worse utility that happens to share a name with the average one. Reliability equity work begins exactly there, at the gap between the index and the address.

A 500 kVA distribution transformer in Ossbury currently carries 437 kVA at peak, and its load is growing at 3 percent per year. What is its current loading percentage, and in about how many years does it reach full rating?

The transformer is loaded to 87.4 percent today, and at 3 percent compound growth it reaches its 500 kVA rating in about 4.6 years. The logarithm is doing real work here — growth to a ceiling is an exponential question, and the intuitive linear guess (the remaining 63 kVA divided by this year's 13 kVA of growth) understates the timeline's compression because each year's growth is larger than the last. In practice the utility will not wait for 100 percent. Transformers tolerate overload poorly in summer heat, lose insulation life rapidly when run hot, and are planned against a loading threshold — often 80 to 90 percent at peak — precisely so that a failed unit's load can be picked up by its neighbors. So the 4.6 year figure is really a deadline minus a safety margin: the replacement or the load transfer belongs on a capital plan roughly a year before the arithmetic says the ceiling arrives. There is also a subtlety in the growth rate itself: 3 percent on this transformer usually means a specific subdivision filling in or a few large customers arriving, not a smooth demographic tide. Planners who know which rooftops are causing the growth can forecast it; planners who only know the percentage are extrapolating a rumor. The equation is exact. Its input is a judgment.

Give me a structured comparison of the three feeder configurations a distribution utility like the fictional Kestrel Falls Electric might use: radial, looped, and networked. Cover how each is built, how each handles a fault, and what each costs.

Kestrel Falls Electric's three distribution architectures:

| Configuration | How it is built | Behavior on a fault | Cost profile |
|---|---|---|---|
| Radial | One path from substation to customer, branching like a tree | Everything downstream of the fault stays dark until repair or manual switching | Cheapest to build and protect; standard for suburbs and rural areas |
| Looped | Feeders arranged in a ring, operated open at one point | Crews (or automated switches) open both sides of the fault and backfeed the healthy sections from the other direction; most customers restored in minutes to an hour | Moderate — extra conductor, switches, and protection coordination |
| Networked | Multiple interconnected paths with automatic protection, typical under dense downtowns | Fault is isolated by its own protectors with no customer interruption in most cases | Most expensive by far; justified only where outage costs are extreme |

The choice is an insurance decision expressed in copper. A radial system spends nothing on redundancy and pays in outage minutes; a network spends heavily and pays almost never. What decides is the cost of darkness per customer — a radial feeder serving farms and a network serving hospitals, exchanges, and a financial district are not inconsistent choices but the same calculation at different prices. The industry trend is to blur the middle: looped systems with automated switching buy most of the network's restoration speed at a fraction of its cost, which is why the plain radial feeder, unassisted, is quietly becoming the budget option rather than the standard.

Kestrel Falls Electric operates 210 miles of overhead line faulting at 0.14 faults per mile per year with a 4.5-hour average repair, and 60 miles of underground cable faulting at 0.05 per mile per year with a 14-hour average repair. Compare the expected annual fault counts and the total repair-hours each plant generates.

Overhead plant generates 29.4 faults a year; underground generates 3. In repair time the comparison narrows dramatically: the overhead faults consume 132.3 crew-hours annually, the underground faults 42 — so undergrounding cuts fault frequency by nearly ninety percent per mile but each event costs three times the hours to fix. This is the honest shape of the undergrounding debate, which is usually argued with only half the numbers. Overhead faults are frequent, visible, and quick: a crew can see the damage from the truck, and most are trees, lightning, and vehicles — external insults to an exposed plant. Underground faults are rare, invisible, and slow: the cable must be located, fault-traced, excavated, spliced in a hole, and tested, and the failure is usually the plant's own aging rather than an insult. Customers experience the difference as character, not totals: overhead neighborhoods get many short outages, underground neighborhoods get almost none and then a very long one. Which profile a city prefers depends on what its outages cost per hour — and on whether it is pricing the conversion honestly, since burying a mile of line costs several times what the overhead mile cost, a premium that buys fault avoidance, not fault immunity.

During a generation shortfall, Alverton's utility must be ready to shed 46 megawatts. Its rotating outage blocks are built at about 9 megawatts each, and each block is held out for 45 minutes before being restored and the next block dropped. How many blocks must be prepared, and how long does a full rotation take?

The utility needs 6 blocks prepared — five blocks give only 45 megawatts, one short of the requirement, so the ceiling rounds up — and a full rotation through all 6 blocks takes 270 minutes, or 4.5 hours. Rotating outages are an exercise in distributing a shortage fairly under time pressure, and the design choices are all visible in these numbers. Block size trades precision against practicality: smaller blocks shed closer to the exact requirement but multiply switching operations and the chance of error at the worst possible moment. The 45-minute hold is a compromise between mercy and grid physics — long enough to be worth the switching, short enough that no neighborhood's outage becomes a health event. The rotation length is the number customers actually experience as fairness: at 4.5 hours, a customer in a shed block can expect the burden to come back around on a knowable cycle, and the utility can publish it. Hidden inside the block construction is the hardest work: critical loads — hospitals, water plants, 911 centers — are wired out of the blocks entirely, which means the blocks must be assembled from the feeders that remain, and their sizes come out ragged no matter how round the plan says 9 megawatts is.

A demand-response program in Varenne has 12,400 enrolled homes. Each can shed an average of 0.9 kilowatts when called, but only 72 percent of the enrolled capacity is expected to respond at any given event (the coincidence factor). The grid operator wants 10 megawatts. What shed can the program actually promise, and what is the shortfall?

Nameplate enrollment is 11160 kilowatts, but after the coincidence factor the program can honestly promise 8035 kilowatts — 8.04 megawatts — leaving a shortfall of 1.96 megawatts against the operator's 10. The coincidence factor is where demand-response marketing goes to die. Enrollment counts thermostats and water heaters that signed a form; coincidence counts the ones that are home, running, connected, and not overridden at 4 p.m. on the hottest day of the year — which is, not coincidentally, exactly when the shed is needed and exactly when participants are most tempted to opt out. Serious program planning therefore works backward from the promised number, not forward from enrollment: to promise 10 megawatts at this coincidence and per-home shed, the program would need roughly 15,400 enrolled homes, and recruiting materials that quote the nameplate 11160 kilowatts are borrowing credibility the event day will repossess. None of this makes demand response weak — 8.04 megawatts delivered in minutes, with no fuel and no new wires, is a genuinely valuable resource. It makes it a resource that must be derated like any other, by people willing to say the smaller number in the planning meeting and the larger one only in the brochure's footnotes.

A substation in Dunmore has two 40 MVA transformers. Under the N-1 standard the station must survive losing one unit, so its firm capacity is the capacity of a single transformer. Peak load is 36.5 MVA and growing at 1.8 MVA per year. What percentage of firm capacity is the station at, and how long until load reaches firm capacity?

The station is already at 91.25 percent of firm capacity, with 1.9 years of growth headroom left. N-1 is the reliability bargain stated as arithmetic: the station owns 80 MVA of iron but may only plan on 40, because the second transformer is not capacity — it is the spare that makes the first one's promise good. To a ratepayer this can look like waste, a substation running at half its nameplate. To an operator it is the difference between a transformer failure being an internal event and it being a neighborhood's week. The 1.9 year horizon is the number that should be setting off quiet alarms, because the remedies all have long lead times: a replacement transformer is a bespoke, year-plus procurement; transferring load to neighboring stations requires those stations to have headroom of their own; and the load growth itself — driven here by development already approved — will not politely pause. Stations do not usually fail their standard in a crisis. They erode toward it, one subdivision at a time, in planning documents anyone could read, until the year the peak arrives and the standard is discovered to have been spent. The percentage is the warning. It only works if someone is watching it while there is still time to act on what it says.

Outage blocks A through F each shed 9 megawatts, rotating so consecutive windows drop consecutive blocks. Simulate the event and report each block's unserved energy and the total.

A 0.0
B 0.0
C 0.0
D 0.0
E 6.75
