total unserved MWh: 13.5

The simulation's per-block unserved energy and the event total are printed above — the total comes to 13.5 MWh. Read the pattern, not just the sum. The first four windows need no shedding at all, because load stays at or under the 46-megawatt ceiling; the event is entirely a creature of the last two windows, when load climbs past firm capacity. In window five the deficit is a single megawatt, yet a whole 9-megawatt block must drop — shedding is quantized, and the grid cannot shave a megawatt off a feeder, only take feeders whole. That quantization is why rotating outages always overshoot the deficit and why block size is such a contested design choice. The rotation assigns the two deficit windows to consecutive blocks in the sequence, so the burden lands on different neighborhoods rather than returning to the first block while it is still dark from its previous turn. Unserved energy is the honest scorecard for all of it: not how many customers were out, or for how long in the abstract, but how many megawatt-hours of life — refrigeration, medical devices, elevators, light — did not happen. Fairness in a shortage is the art of distributing that number so no one address accumulates it twice.
Two streetlight questions from a resident meeting: why don't the lights just run on timers, and what does the crew mean when they report a 'knockdown'?

Timers seem simpler until the year starts moving. A streetlight's job is to burn from dusk to dawn, and dusk migrates by hours across the seasons — a timer set right in June is lighting empty streets in daylight by December and leaving dark ones unlit in the morning. Timers also drift, fail silently after power outages, and must be visited to be corrected. A photocell solves all of it by measuring the thing itself: it switches the light on when ambient light falls below a threshold and off when it rises, automatically tracking seasons, storms, and even the gloom of an eclipse, with no clock to set. The knockdown is simpler and sadder: it is a pole struck by a vehicle and knocked down or snapped at its base. Poles are deliberately built with breakaway bases so the car wins the argument and the occupants survive it, which means the pole's destruction is the safety feature working. A knockdown is therefore both a lighting outage and a traffic incident — the crew's response includes making the electrical service safe, since a downed pole can leave live conductors at ankle height, before anyone thinks about restoring the light. Residents report the dark street; the utility hears the word knockdown and dispatches as if it were a crash scene, because it was one.

East Sollis is converting 8,400 streetlights from 150-watt high-pressure sodium fixtures to 62-watt LEDs. The lights burn 4,150 hours per year and electricity costs $0.117 per kilowatt-hour. What is the annual energy saving per fixture, across the city, and in dollars?

Each conversion saves 365.2 kilowatt-hours a year — the 88-watt reduction running for 4,150 hours. Across 8,400 fixtures that is 3067680 kilowatt-hours, worth about $358919 annually at the city's rate. The energy figure, large as it is, is usually not the strongest line in the conversion case. Sodium fixtures need relamping and ballast work on a three-to-five-year cycle, with a bucket truck and a crew for every visit, while an LED fixture's rated life stretches past a decade of nights — so the maintenance saving, spread over thousands of poles, rivals the power saving and is far more predictable. The conversion also changes the failure politics: sodium lamps die one at a time, constantly, generating the steady drip of outage reports residents judge the city by, while LEDs tend to fail rarely and in batches tied to a bad production run or a surge. There is a genuine trade buried in the triumph, though — the city is swapping a mature, well-understood technology whose light some residents prefer for an electronic one whose drivers age in ways the industry is still learning. The spreadsheet wins anyway, at $358919 a year. But the honest proposal mentions that the city is also buying a new learning curve.
Ternwick has 214 reported streetlight outages in its backlog. Its crews repair 38 lights per day, but residents report 26 new outages per day. How long until the backlog clears at this rate?

The crews are gaining on the backlog at only 12 lights per day net, so clearing 214 takes 17.8 days. This is the arithmetic of every municipal backlog, and it explains why they feel permanent even when everyone is working hard: what matters is not the repair rate of 38 a day, which sounds vigorous, but the margin of 12 over the inflow. The backlog is a bathtub, and the drain is barely wider than the tap. The management options follow directly from the equation. Raise the repair rate with a second crew or a contractor surge and the clearance time falls proportionally — doubling the net gain halves the wait. Reduce the inflow and the same crews win faster, which is why a district-wide LED conversion or a cable-fault repair program can clear a backlog without a single extra repair visit: it turns off the tap. Or shrink the definition — some of the 214 are duplicates, lights on private property, or outages already fixed but never closed in the system, and auditing the list is the cheapest crew of all. What does not work is exhortation. A backlog with a net gain of 12 a day clears in 17.8 days no matter how urgently anyone speaks about it, and a manager who promises otherwise is negotiating with arithmetic.

Give me a structured comparison of the three street lighting technologies in the fictional city of Ossbury's inventory: high-pressure sodium, LED, and induction. Cover typical wattage for arterial lighting, rated life, light quality, and maintenance pattern. Use the city's planning figures.

Ossbury's street lighting inventory, by technology:

| Technology | Typical arterial wattage | Rated life | Light quality | Maintenance pattern |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| High-pressure sodium | 150–250 W | 24,000 hours | Orange, poor color rendering — faces and car colors wash out | Group relamping every 4–5 years plus constant spot failures |
| LED | 60–110 W | 100,000 hours | White, good color rendering; color temperature is a policy choice | Very low routine maintenance; failures are electronic and batch-prone |
| Induction | 100–165 W | 60,000 hours | White, decent rendering | Rarely fails, but parts and expertise are now scarce as the market moved to LED |

The table tells a technology-transition story. Sodium's real cost was never its electricity alone but the perpetual relamping treadmill — a city of thousands of poles was always mid-cycle, with a fraction of its lights dead at any moment. LED broke the treadmill and cut wattage by more than half, at the price of making light quality a political decision: the same fixture family can be ordered in warm or harsh color temperatures, and neighborhoods notice. Induction is the cautionary tale — a genuinely good technology orphaned when the industry standardized elsewhere, leaving its owners with reliable lamps and an unreliable supply chain. Cities do not choose lighting technologies; they choose which decade's maintenance problem they would rather have.

A 1.9-mile arterial in Halloway is to be relit with poles spaced 135 feet apart, staggered on both sides. How many poles does the design need (round each side up), and what is the installed cost at $4,850 per pole?

The run needs 74.3 pole positions per side, which rounds up to 75 per side and 150 poles total in the staggered layout — an installed cost of $727500. Spacing is where lighting design stops being about light and becomes about everything else. The 135-foot figure comes from the photometric calculation — the spacing at which pools of light from adjacent fixtures overlap enough that no dark band crosses the roadway — but the pole count it produces then drives the project's real constraints: each pole is a foundation, a potential knockdown, a future maintenance visit, and an object in the clear zone that road-safety standards have opinions about. Staggering the poles, rather than facing them in pairs, halves the visual rhythm and evens the light, at the cost of running conductor and foundations on both sides of the street. Notice the rounding: 74.3 positions per side cannot be built, so the design buys 75 and quietly tightens the actual spacing a few feet. Street lighting budgets are full of these small honest roundings, each invisible, summing to real money — the difference between the photometric ideal and the buildable street is where engineering judgment lives.

Ossbury owns 26,500 streetlights and wants every light inspected once per 5-year cycle. A night-inspection crew can survey 46 lights per night, works 4 nights a week, 46 weeks a year. How many inspections per year does the cycle require, what is the crew's annual capacity, and what utilization does the program run at?

The cycle requires 5300 inspections a year. One crew delivers 8464 inspections a year, so the program runs at 62.6 percent of a single crew's capacity — feasible with room to spare. The spare room is not waste; it is what absorbs the program's real frictions. Night inspection is weather-limited in ways the 46-week year only partly captures, the crew is the same one pulled onto knockdowns and outage verification, and a survey's value depends on the defects found being fed into repair queues that have their own backlogs. Running at 62.6 percent also leaves the crew able to re-inspect repaired districts within the same cycle, which is what turns inspection from a census into quality control. The deeper point is what the cycle buys. A city that inspects on a five-year rhythm learns its failure rate as data rather than as resident complaints — it discovers the bad production batch, the corroding pole district, the photocell vintage that fails early — while a city that only responds to reports is sampling its lighting quality through whoever phones in, which is a biased instrument pointed at the neighborhoods with the most time to complain. Proactive inspection is unglamorous. It is also the difference between managing an asset and being managed by it.

Varenne's permit office receives 46 applications per working day, and the average application spends 23 working days in the system from submission to decision. Using Little's law, how many applications are in process at any given time?

Little's law gives 1058 applications in process — arrival rate times time in system. The law's power is that it needs nothing else: no staffing model, no process map, just the two numbers any permit office already knows, and it returns the inventory the office is carrying whether it admits to carrying it or not. That inventory is the real experience of the system. Applicants do not feel the 23 days as an abstraction; they feel it as 1,058 files ahead of and behind them, each one a kitchen remodel, a sign, a small business opening whose financing is priced by the month. Little's law also hands managers their only three levers, because the equation has only three terms. Cut arrivals — pre-application screening that stops hopeless filings — and inventory falls. Cut time in system and it falls. Or hold both and accept the inventory, which is a decision too, though rarely an admitted one. What the law forbids is the fourth option every office wishes for: promising faster decisions at the same volume with the same process. The arithmetic has no term for effort or intentions. It is the queue, stating its terms.
Why do building permits take so long when each individual review — zoning, structural, fire — only takes a few days? Where does the time actually go?

Mostly into the spaces between the reviews, not the reviews themselves. In a traditional sequential system, your application is not being examined by three departments in a few days each; it is being examined for a few days, then waiting in the next department's inbox for weeks, then examined, then waiting again. The file spends the overwhelming majority of its life in queues, untouched, and each handoff adds the receiving department's backlog to your timeline. Worse, sequential review creates the correction cascade: the fire reviewer, seeing the file last, requests a change that invalidates the structural approval already granted, and the application loops back to the start of a queue it already waited through once. Parallel review — all departments examining simultaneously, against a shared deadline, with conflicts resolved in one coordination meeting — attacks exactly this structure. The reviews themselves take the same few days; what disappears is the serial waiting and most of the cascade, because conflicts surface while everyone is still at the table. The reason it is not universal is that parallel review is harder to manage: it requires departments to staff to a common rhythm instead of their own, and to surrender the quiet power of the inbox. When a permit office announces its reviewers 'only take three days,' it is telling the truth about the work and omitting the truth about the wait. Your permit was not slow because it was examined slowly. It was slow because it was, for most of its life, not being examined at all.
Dunmore's permit backlog is 1,340 applications. Reviewers complete 58 per day while 47 new ones arrive per day. How long does the backlog take to clear, in working days and in five-day working weeks?

The office gains only 11 applications a day on the backlog, so clearing 1,340 takes 121.8 working days — 24.4 working weeks, the better part of half a year. This is why backlog announcements so often disappoint: the public hears 'we process 58 a day' and imagines the pile gone in three weeks, because the intuitive denominator is the completion rate, not the margin. The margin is the truth, and a margin of 11 against an inflow of 47 is fragile — lose two reviewers to vacancies and the margin inverts; the backlog starts growing again while the office is, by every internal measure, working at full capacity. Serious backlog programs therefore attack the margin from both sides at once: surge completions with overtime or contract reviewers, and throttle arrivals with better pre-screening so incomplete applications stop entering the count at all. There is also a composition trap inside the 1,340: backlogs are never uniform, and the easy applications get cleared first, so the average difficulty of the remainder rises as the count falls. The last 200 files will be the oldest, strangest, and most disputed. A clearance curve that assumes a constant rate is lying by the halfway point — the honest plan prices the tail.

Give me a structured breakdown of the stages a building permit passes through in the fictional city of Alverton: what each stage checks, its typical duration, and its first-pass success rate. Use the city's published planning figures.

Alverton's permit pipeline, stage by stage:

| Stage | What it checks | Typical duration | First-pass success |
|---|---|---|---|
| Intake & completeness | Forms, fees, drawings present and legible | 2 days | 78% |
| Zoning review | Use, setbacks, height, parking against the district code | 5 days | 84% |
| Structural review | Loads, foundations, framing, seismic and wind details | 8 days | 71% |
| Fire & life safety | Egress, sprinklers, alarms, fire separation | 6 days | 76% |
| Health & utilities | Water, sewer, grease, backflow where applicable | 4 days | 88% |
| Issuance | Final fees, conditions, permit card and inspections schedule | 1 day | 97% |

Read the first-pass column as the pipeline's confession. Even a well-run office sends roughly a quarter of applications back at the structural stage, and every return restarts a queue somewhere upstream — which is why total elapsed time is two to three times the sum of the durations in the middle column. The stages with the lowest first-pass rates are the ones where applicants most need guidance before they file, and where pre-application meetings earn their keep. Issuance's 97 percent is the tell that the system works as a filter: by the time a file reaches the last desk, it has been corrected into compliance. The permit was never really granted at issuance. It was granted gradually, correction by correction, at every desk that sent it back.

Of 1,240 permit applications in Kestrel Falls last year, 38 percent were sent back for corrections at least once, and each correction cycle adds an average of 12 days. How many applications cycled back, and what is the average delay added across all applications?

471 applications went back for corrections, and averaged across all 1,240 filings the correction process adds 4.56 days per application. That expected-value figure is the fairest way to price a quality problem, because it spreads the pain of the unlucky 38 percent across the whole population the way the office's workload actually experiences it. But it conceals the distribution, and the distribution is where applicants live: 62 percent of filers sail through, while the cycling minority does not experience 4.56 days — they experience 12, and sometimes 24 if the corrected plans draw a second round of comments, which the 38 percent figure quietly includes repeat cyclers within. The policy lever follows from the arithmetic. Cutting the correction rate is worth more than speeding the correction cycle, because the rate multiplies everything downstream: fewer cycles mean fewer re-reviews, shorter queues for everyone, and fewer projects whose financing dies during a second loop. This is why the highest-yield investment in a permit office is usually not reviewers but the unglamorous front end — checklists written in plain language, example drawings of compliant details, pre-application meetings for the project types that cycle most. Every application that files correctly the first time is twelve days the system never has to spend.

Alverton wants its average permit time down to 10 working days at an arrival rate of 52 applications per day. Current work-in-process is 910 applications. Reviewers each complete 6.5 applications per day and there are 11 reviewers. Using Little's law, what WIP does the target imply, how much excess WIP must drain, and how long does draining take at the current staffing?

The 10-day target at 52 arrivals a day implies a work-in-process of 520 applications. The office is carrying 910, so 390 applications of excess inventory must drain. Eleven reviewers complete 71.5 applications a day against 52 arrivals, a surplus of 19.5 a day, so the drain takes about 20 working days. The satisfying part of this plan is that it ends in equilibrium: once WIP reaches 520, the same staffing that drained the backlog holds the 10-day average indefinitely, because the surplus that did the draining becomes the buffer that absorbs bad weeks. The unsatisfying part is everything the arithmetic assumes away. It assumes the 6.5-per-day reviewer rate survives contact with the backlog's hardest files — it will not, because excess WIP is disproportionately old, disputed, and weird. It assumes arrivals hold at 52 through a construction season that has never once held at anything. And it assumes nobody raids the surplus capacity mid-drain for a priority project, which in a real city hall is the single most reliable prediction available. Treat the 20 days as the floor of the timeline, the answer if the world cooperates. Then manage the drain like it matters, because the plan's real content is not the date — it is the discovery that the office was carrying nearly double the inventory its own service promise allows.

Halloway processed 3,900 permit applications last year. Under paper intake, 14 percent contained errors that generated rework averaging 0.8 staff-hours each. The new online portal's validation cuts the error rate to 5 percent. How many staff-hours does the portal save per year, and how many 40-hour staff-weeks is that?

Paper intake produced 546 error cases; the portal produces 195. The avoided rework is 280.8 staff-hours a year — 7 staff-weeks. The mechanism matters more than the total. Paper intake does not merely permit errors; it defers their discovery to the most expensive possible moment, after a reviewer has opened the file, understood it, and found the missing form or the illegible dimension — at which point the reviewer's partial work is discarded and the file rejoins a queue. Portal validation moves the same discovery to the moment of typing, when the applicant can fix it in seconds and the file never enters the system broken. This is the general shape of digitization gains that actually materialize: not doing the old work faster, but refusing to accept work that will have to be done twice. The staff-weeks figure also deserves honest framing — 7 weeks is not a person who can be fired; it is fragments of hundreds of days returned to reviewers, which the office will spend on the backlog, where it converts directly into shorter waits. The portal did not save money, exactly. It saved the only currency a permit office really trades in: reviewer attention, previously burned on other people's typos.

Varenne's permit office starts a month with a backlog of 240 applications and can complete 55 per day. Daily arrivals for the 30 working days follow the fixed list in the simulation. Run it and report the ending backlog, the peak backlog, and the net change.

arguments.code:
backlog = 240
arrivals = [58, 61, 57, 63, 59, 56, 62, 58, 60, 55, 48, 44, 50, 46, 52, 45, 49, 43, 51, 47, 44, 50, 46, 48, 45, 52, 47, 49, 44, 50]
capacity = 55
peak = backlog
for day in range(30):
    backlog = backlog + arrivals[day] - capacity
    peak = max(peak, backlog)
print('ending backlog:', backlog)
print('peak backlog:', peak)
print('net change over 30 days:', sum(arrivals) - 30*capacity)

peak backlog: 279

The month ends with the backlog at 129, having peaked at 279, for a net change of -111 applications. The interesting number is the peak, not the ending. Capacity exceeds average arrivals, so the month is a winning one on paper — yet the backlog still climbs well above its starting point during the opening surge, because arrivals arrive in weather, not in averages: a ten-day run averaging nearly 59 applications a day lands faster than the fixed completion rate can drain, and the queue remembers every surge for days after the surge ends. This is the daily reality behind every service-level statistic. An office can be correctly staffed for the month and still breach its promised turnaround in the month's worst week, because promises are kept or broken on individual applications, and an application filed the morning of a surge inherits the whole accumulated queue. The simulation also shows why managers hoard surge capacity so jealously — overtime authorized after the peak is visible is worth half as much as the same hours worked during it. Queues have memory. Staffing plans that ignore the peak line are planning for a month that never occurs.
What does it mean when a fire department talks about a unit's 'first-due' area?

The first-due area is the territory for which a particular unit — an engine, a ladder, a medic — is the designated first responder: the area it is expected to reach first and handle as its own. Every address in the city sits inside several overlapping first-due maps at once, one per unit type, so your house is in Engine 7's first-due, Ladder 3's first-due, and Medic 12's first-due simultaneously. The maps are drawn from station locations and road networks, and they drive far more than dispatch. Call volume by first-due area is how a department knows which stations are earning their keep and which are idle; response-time statistics are reported by first-due area, which is how a neighborhood learns it is the slow corner of the city; and when a new station is proposed, the entire argument is conducted in redrawn first-due maps. The concept also creates the system's characteristic awkwardness at boundaries: an incident fifty feet inside Engine 7's area gets Engine 7 even if Engine 5's crew is closer today because it happens to be returning from another call — though modern dispatch systems increasingly soften this with closest-unit recommendations. First-due is the department's theory of its own geography, written in advance. Every response is that theory meeting the day's facts.

An engine company in Dunmore must cover an address 1.5 miles from the station. Apparatus average 28 mph on the street network. Dispatch processing takes 0.9 minutes and turnout (crew gearing up and rolling) takes 1.3 minutes. What is the total response time, and how does it compare with the department's 8-minute 90th-percentile target?

Travel time is 3.2 minutes, and the full response — dispatch, turnout, travel — totals 5.4 minutes, comfortably inside the 8-minute target. The decomposition is the useful part, because each component has a different owner and a different physics. Dispatch time belongs to the call center and shrinks with staffing and protocol design. Turnout belongs to the station — its layout, its alerting system, whether the crew is awake — and is the most human of the three. Travel belongs to geography and traffic, and it is the only component that grows worse as the city succeeds: denser development means more calls but also slower streets. Note also what the 90th-percentile framing admits. The department does not promise 8 minutes; it promises that nine responses in ten beat 8 minutes, which quietly licenses the tenth — the address at the district's edge, during the storm, when the first-due engine is already out. Averages would hide that tenth response entirely. The fractile standard forces the system to confess its worst decile, and station-location arguments are really arguments about who gets to live in it.
Engine 7 in Varenne runs 14.2 calls per day averaging 38 minutes each. How many hours per day is the unit committed, and what is its unit hour utilization (share of the 24-hour day committed)?

Engine 7 is committed for 539.6 minutes a day — 8.99 hours — a unit hour utilization of 0.375. UHU is the fire service's workload thermometer, and 0.375 sits in the band departments watch carefully. The naive reading — the crew is idle five-eighths of the day — misses what the uncommitted time is for. Calls do not arrive on a schedule; they arrive in clusters, and a unit already committed when its district calls is a unit that does not respond, exporting the call to a farther station at a worse time. Reliability is a function of availability at the random instant, and availability falls off a cliff as utilization climbs: past roughly 0.35 to 0.40, a unit is so often busy that its first-due area is effectively covered by its neighbors, and response times district-wide degrade together. The uncommitted hours also hold the training, inspections, maintenance, and rest that keep the committed hours competent — a crew run at the redline for months gets slower and more error-prone inside the calls themselves. UHU therefore reads like a blood pressure: some is health, more is performance, and too much is a diagnosis. The number that looks like slack is the system's surge capacity, and it is spent exactly once — on the worst day, which is the day it was for.

The fictional city of Braddock Vale covers 96 square miles. A station's effective coverage is a circle of radius 2.2 miles, but circles do not tile a city — overlapping coverage and road geometry mean each station effectively covers its circle divided by an overlap factor of 1.35. How many stations does the geometry suggest, and how does that compare with the city's current 7?

One station's circle covers 15.21 square miles, so naive division suggests 6.3 stations, and applying the overlap factor raises the requirement to 8.5 — call it 9 stations against the current 7. The gap between the naive 6.3 and the corrected figure is where station politics lives. Circles overlap because they must: a city is not a honeycomb, stations sit on real land along real roads, and the areas between circles — the lens-shaped gaps at the edges of three districts — are precisely where the worst response times accumulate. The overlap factor is a confession that geometry charges a tax of about a third. A two-station deficit, then, does not distribute itself evenly as slightly slower service everywhere. It concentrates in the gap neighborhoods, which experience a different fire department from the one in the brochure. This is why coverage studies map the uncovered pockets by name rather than reporting a citywide average: the average citizen of Braddock Vale is fine, and the specific citizens in the lens gaps are not, and both statements are computed from the same map. The arithmetic says 9. The map says where the missing two belong.

Give me a structured comparison of the four front-line unit types in the fictional Dunmore Fire Department: engine, ladder, medic, and heavy rescue. Cover crew size, primary role, and share of the department's call volume. Use the department's published figures.

Dunmore's front-line fleet, by unit type:

| Unit | Crew | Primary role | Share of call volume |
|---|---|---|---|
| Engine | 4 | Fire suppression — carries water, hose, and a pump | 31% |
| Ladder (truck) | 4 | Aerial access, ventilation, search, forcible entry at height | 12% |
| Medic (ambulance) | 2 | Emergency medical response and transport | 49% |
| Heavy rescue | 3 | Vehicle extrication, collapse, confined space, technical rescue | 8% |

The call-volume column explains the modern fire department better than its name does. Nearly half the work is medical, which is why medic units — the cheapest crew on the list — carry the system's heaviest load, and why departments cross-staff and cross-train relentlessly: an engine company spends much of its day as a first-response medical unit that occasionally fights fires. The engine and ladder remain the irreducible core, because the 31 percent and 12 percent include the calls where minutes decide outcomes and no substitute exists. Heavy rescue is the insurance policy — 8 percent of calls, but the ones where the wrong equipment means the incident cannot be worked at all. Read together, the table is a portfolio: high-frequency low-complexity work funding, in attention and budget, the low-frequency high-complexity capability that justifies the department's existence on its worst day.

In Alverton's busiest hour last month, 9 calls arrived in the same district and the average call committed a unit for 47 minutes. How many unit-hours of work did that single hour generate, and what does it imply for a district staffed with 5 units?

That one hour generated 423 unit-minutes — 7.05 unit-hours of committed work. A district with 5 units owns exactly 5 unit-hours per clock hour, so the busiest hour's demand exceeded the district's entire theoretical supply by more than 40 percent — before accounting for the fact that calls arrive simultaneously rather than in a tidy queue. In practice the excess is absorbed three ways, none free. Neighboring districts' units respond in, degrading their own coverage and lengthening their next response. Some calls wait, and the wait concentrates in the least severe categories by design — the alarm with no smoke holds while the reported structure fire rolls. And crews' committed time stretches, as units clear one call and take the next without returning, which is efficient until it is exhaustion. This is why staffing to the average hour is a fiction departments cannot afford: demand is spiky at exactly the scale staffing is decided. The average hour in this district might need 2 unit-hours. The busiest needs 7.05. A fire department is built, staffed, and judged at the peak — the average merely pays the bills between peaks.

A dispatch center in Ossbury handles 214 calls per day, and the busiest hour carries 11 percent of the day's calls. Three call-takers staff that hour, and answering plus processing each call takes 74 seconds of a call-taker's time. How loaded is each call-taker during the peak hour?

The peak hour brings 23.5 calls, or 7.8 per call-taker, consuming 581 seconds of each hour — about 16 percent utilization. On paper that looks like slack, and it is the most dangerous kind of number in emergency operations, because the average conceals the arrival pattern. Calls do not arrive every seven minutes like a metronome; they arrive in bursts — a single highway pileup can generate a dozen calls in ninety seconds, all reporting the same incident, all needing to be answered, triaged, and deduplicated while a genuine second emergency competes for the same ears. At 16 percent average load the center has the reserve to absorb those bursts, which is precisely what the reserve is for. Staff the hour to 90 percent average utilization and the queueing mathematics turns vicious: wait times do not grow linearly with load, they explode, and the caller who hears ringing instead of an answer is experiencing a staffing model, not bad luck. Dispatch is the one part of the response chain where the resource is attention, and attention queues exactly like everything else in this batch — the only difference is that the queue is invisible until someone is listening to it ring.

Kestrel Falls is modeling the closure of Station B, which handles 1,860 calls a year. Neighboring stations would absorb them: A takes 720, C takes 640, D takes 500. Response time in B's old area rises from 5.1 to 7.8 minutes. Verify the absorption adds up, and compute the effect on the citywide average response time across the city's 21,400 annual calls.

The absorption checks out: 1860 calls redistributed, exactly B's volume. The citywide average response time, however, rises by only 0.23 minutes — about fourteen seconds — because B's worsening is diluted across all 21,400 city calls. Both numbers are true, and the distance between them is the entire politics of station closures. The city's presentation will quote the 0.23: a rounding error, a reasonable efficiency. B's neighborhood will quote its own figure: 2.7 minutes added to every response in an area that did nothing to deserve a slower fire department, concentrated in the minutes where cardiac arrests and room fires are decided. Averages are how institutions distribute blame until it disappears; distributions are how residents experience the decision. There is also a second-order effect the static model misses — A, C, and D absorbing 1,860 extra calls raises their utilization, which lowers their availability for their own areas, so the true cost leaks outward in ways the single-number model understates. The honest closure analysis publishes the neighborhood distribution, the utilization effects, and the savings in the same table. A city that only publishes the 0.23 has not done the analysis. It has done the advocacy.

Last year Marrowgate's fire department gave 132 mutual-aid responses to neighboring towns and received 88. The regional compact values a response at $310 for settlement purposes. What is the net balance in responses and in dollars, and why do compacts track it?

Marrowgate is a net giver by 44 responses, worth $13640 at the compact's rate. Mutual aid runs on a deliberate fiction — that help between neighboring departments is reciprocal and need not be invoiced — and the balance sheet exists to keep the fiction honest. Small asymmetries are the system working: fires do not respect either borders or fairness, and this year's net giver is next year's beneficiary when the warehouse fire lands on the other side of the line. But a persistent, growing imbalance is information. It usually means one town is under-building its own capacity and quietly importing its neighbors' — enjoying a lower tax rate subsidized by the next town's stations — or that growth has shifted the region's risk and the compact's map no longer matches it. The $310 rate is not really a price; a true response costs far more in crew time, wear, and coverage left behind. It is a unit of account, a way to make generosity legible so it can be discussed before it curdles into resentment. The departments that track the balance annually, and settle it in training, equipment, or staffing rather than cash, are the ones whose mutual aid survives contact with a bad year. Aid that is never counted eventually gets counted by someone, angrily, at the worst moment.

Simulate a 60-call shift for a four-unit district in Halloway: calls arrive with an average gap of 0.22 hours (exponential), each call commits a unit for 0.4 to 1.1 hours (uniform), using random seed 7. Report how many calls had to wait for a unit, the maximum number of units busy at once, and the longest wait.

arguments.code:
import random
random.seed(7)
units_free_at = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]   # four units, times in hours from shift start
waits = []
busy_max = 0
t = 0.0
for call in range(60):
    t += random.expovariate(1/0.22)          # average one call per 0.22 hours
    duration = random.uniform(0.4, 1.1)      # hours committed
    unit = min(range(4), key=lambda u: units_free_at[u])
    start = max(t, units_free_at[unit])
    waits.append(start - t)
    units_free_at[unit] = start + duration
    busy = sum(1 for u in units_free_at if u > t)
    busy_max = max(busy_max, busy)
waited = sum(1 for w in waits if w > 0.01)
print('calls that waited:', waited)
print('max simultaneous units busy:', busy_max)
print('longest wait (min):', round(max(waits)*60, 1))

messages.content:
calls that waited: 39
max simultaneous units busy: 4
longest wait (min): 69.3

In the simulated shift, 39 of 60 calls arrived to find every unit committed and had to wait, the district hit a maximum of 4 units busy simultaneously, and the longest wait reached 69.3 minutes. The average workload in this simulation is well within the roster on paper — the offered load works out to about 3.4 units' worth of work against four units — yet a four-unit district still leaves most callers in this run waiting at least briefly, because arrivals are Poisson: they cluster by pure chance, and a cluster that lands while durations run long exhausts the roster through no one's failure. This is the mathematical reason emergency coverage cannot be staffed to its average, and it is worth being precise about the intuition it corrects. People imagine that if the district's units are busy about 85 percent of capacity, a new call finds help most of the time. In fact the probability that all units are simultaneously busy is far higher than the idle fraction suggests — queueing systems have a knee, and emergency services live deliberately on the safe side of it, paying for idle hours as the premium on never hearing the words 'no unit available.' The simulation's seed makes it reproducible; change it and the counts wobble, but the shape — a waiting minority produced by pure randomness at moderate load — is in every seed. That shape is the job.
Varenne's 311 system took 1,840 service requests last week: 46 percent by phone, 37 percent by mobile app, and the rest by web. How many requests came through each channel?

Phone brought 846 requests, the app 681, and the web the remaining 313. The split is a portrait of the city filing the report. Phone requests skew older, longer, and more complex — a human conversation can carry a problem that does not fit a form, which is why the phone channel remains the most expensive per request and the hardest to cut. App requests arrive with photographs and GPS coordinates attached, which makes them the cheapest to route and verify, and they skew toward the visible city: potholes, graffiti, broken lights, the defects a person can frame in a picture. The web remainder is the form-fillers, often reporting on behalf of others. The operational trap is to read the channels as interchangeable demand and staff them by volume alone. They are different instruments measuring different cities — app data maps where smartphone owners walk, phone data maps where patience and need coincide, and neither maps the neighborhoods that have stopped reporting at all, whose silence in the data is the most important datum of the three. A 311 dashboard shows a city what its residents complain about. Wisdom is remembering it cannot show what they have given up on.

Give me a structured table of the design life, replacement unit cost, and steady-state annual renewal need for four municipal assets in the fictional city of Ternwick: water mains (1,150 miles), road surfaces (780 lane-miles), signal controllers (340 intersections), and plow trucks (64 units). Use the city's planning figures.

Ternwick's core assets and their renewal arithmetic:

| Asset | Inventory | Design life | Replacement unit cost | Steady-state renewal need |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Water mains | 1,150 miles | 100 years | $1.9M per mile | 11.5 miles per year |
| Road surfaces | 780 lane-miles | 14 years | $310K per lane-mile | 55.7 lane-miles per year |
| Signal controllers | 340 intersections | 20 years | $48K per intersection | 17 intersections per year |
| Plow trucks | 64 units | 12 years | $285K per unit | 5.3 units per year |

Steady-state renewal is the most important column in municipal finance and the least discussed. It says that a city does not own its infrastructure once; it rents it from the future at a rate set by design life, and the rent comes due whether or not the budget acknowledges it. A city renewing below the steady-state rate is not saving money — it is borrowing from its own assets at an interest rate denominated in failures, and the loan compounds, because a water main renewed at year 100 costs the planned price while the same main renewed after it begins breaking costs the planned price plus the breaks. The four assets also run on four different clocks, which is why infrastructure backlogs arrive in waves: a city built in a burst inherits a generation of assets that all reach end-of-life together, and its grandchildren receive the synchronized bill.

Ternwick has 780 lane-miles of road surface with a 14-year resurfacing life, so steady state requires renewing one-fourteenth of the network per year. The budget funds 38 lane-miles per year. What is the steady-state need, and how fast is the backlog growing?

Steady state demands 55.7 lane-miles a year; the budget funds 38, so the backlog grows by 17.7 lane-miles annually. The growth figure understates the damage, because pavement does not deteriorate linearly — it deteriorates on a curve with a cliff in it. A road held in good condition can be kept there cheaply with seals and thin overlays for years; let it slip past the curve's knee and the base fails, converting a resurfacing into a reconstruction at several times the price. The 17.7 lane-miles deferred each year are therefore not a uniform debt. The oldest of them are quietly reclassifying themselves from the cheap column of the budget to the ruinous one, which is why pavement managers preach the doctrine of 'worst-first is wrong': spending the whole budget reconstructing the few failed streets while good streets slide past the knee destroys more network value than it saves. The optimal program feels unjust — it spends visible money on roads that look fine — and it is correct, because the alternative spends invisible money, later, on roads that do not. A backlog measured in lane-miles is a count. A backlog measured in remaining life is a prognosis. Cities need the second number and usually publish the first.

Alverton has 1,150 miles of water main with a nominal 100-year design life. Its renewal program replaces 7.2 miles per year at $1.9 million per mile. What replacement rate does steady state require, what does the current program spend, and how large is the annual gap in miles?

Steady state requires 11.5 miles a year. The current program spends $13.68 million to replace 7.2 miles, leaving an annual gap of 4.3 miles — pipe that ages past its design life every year and joins the de facto backlog. A gap of 4.3 miles a year sounds abstract until it is compounded: a decade of it is 43 miles of main operating on borrowed time, and borrowed time in a water network is repaid in breaks, which arrive at the worst addresses and hours and cost several times the planned replacement price once emergency excavation, water loss, and street restoration are counted. The 100-year design life deserves its own skepticism, too — it is a nominal figure for pipe in average soil, and Alverton's oldest cast iron was laid when the city was a fraction of its size, in ground whose chemistry nobody recorded. The real renewal question is therefore not the arithmetic of the average but the triage of the specific: break history, soil, criticality, and consequence of failure, ranked mile by mile. Steady state sets the budget's size. Condition assessment decides where it lands. A city needs both numbers — the rate that keeps faith with the future, and the map that keeps faith with the present — and the gap between them, stated plainly, is the most honest sentence in its infrastructure report.
